evidence.field: 人 entry; printed p. 698; PDF p. 711
evidence.text: The 人 entry identifies the graph as pictographic, resembling a person in side view, and gives its basic sense as ‘person.’ It describes two early graphic variants—one joining head-like and torso-like parts, another joining head-like and arm-like parts—as equivalent in meaning; it says the former underlies the Shuowen Small Seal form, while the latter was more common in clerical script and developed into regular 人. The attached scan visibly shows the 人 headword, the form sequence, and this explanation. The continuation on PDF p. 712 is the separate 仁 entry, not a continuation of 人.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The record lists oracle-bone example 合集6175, bronze example 集成00944, Chu-script material, and Small Seal / Shuowen material. Its explanation reads 人 as a person standing in profile, interpreting the upper part as head, middle as body, an extended stroke as arm, and lower part as legs. This is the database’s graphic interpretation, not a separately demonstrated stroke chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; 人; shape and examples
evidence.text: The entry describes ancient 人 as a profile figure standing with hands lowered and gives its basic sense as person. It cites oracle-bone examples 《合集》22626 ‘伐十人’ and 《合集》20328 ‘余一人’ (royal self-reference); reports bronze uses glossed ‘common people,’ ‘people,’ and a ruler’s self-reference; and discusses particular uses of 人 for 夷 and 年. The cited loans are source assertions; this entry alone does not independently establish their phonological basis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析: 人

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen explanation of 人 as depicting arm and shin forms and cautions that certain forms called ancient in later references are not found in oracle-bone, bronze, or ancient Zhou-script materials; it says their evidence is unknown. This cautions against using those shapes as established ancestors and does not reject the ordinary profile-person analysis.

The cited oracle-bone and bronze specimens are identified by corpus references, but the inspected sources do not give individual specimen dates or establish the character’s first-use date.

The book and external records support early uses for person, people/common people, and royal self-reference, but do not provide a complete dated semantic chronology or demonstrate every semantic link.

Reports of 人 used for 夷 or 年 are not independently phonologically established in the inspected evidence. The claim that 人 serves as a phonetic element in 年 is distinct from the claim of whole-graph borrowing.
